title: Juvenility, Maturity, and Cutting Competence
objective: Explain how ontogenetic age, tissue position, donor condition, and genotype affect a cutting’s competence to form roots.

terms.definition: An early developmental phase in which tissues express juvenile characteristics and may differ in propagation response from mature tissues.
Developmental progression from juvenile toward mature physiological and morphological states.
The capacity of a tissue to respond to developmental and environmental signals and execute a process such as adventitious rooting.
A shift toward juvenile-like developmental or propagation behavior; it does not by itself imply a change or reset of genotype.
The developmental history of an organism or tissue from its origin through later stages.
A tissue’s functional developmental state as shaped by ontogeny, environment, and management rather than calendar age alone.

coreScience: Juvenility and maturity describe developmental states, not simply calendar age. In many woody and herbaceous plants, juvenile tissues root more readily than mature tissues, but the magnitude and direction of the effect are species- and genotype-dependent.

Within one cannabis mother, shoot position, branch vigor, recent pruning, light exposure, nutritional status, and reproductive history may influence cutting behavior and should be treated as trial variables rather than universal causal factors. Reverted or repeatedly maintained material may show unusual morphology or delayed normalization without necessarily having changed genotype.

Rooting competence is the capacity of a tissue to respond to wound, auxin, carbohydrate, oxygen, moisture, and environmental signals by initiating and developing adventitious roots. It should be evaluated by measured rooting outcomes rather than inferred from labels such as ‘young mother’ or ‘old clone.’
cultivationRelevance: Standardize donor age class, branch position, node number, harvest interval, and mother-management history during trials. Rotate or rehabilitate mothers only after comparing propagation and crop performance.

measureAndRecord.requirement: For Juvenility, Maturity, and Cutting Competence, record donor or batch ID, plant or tray ID, date, operator, source position, starting condition, sanitation step, and any test or quarantine status. Preserve the original controlled note: Controlled record set: Mother age and propagation generation; vegetative or reproductive history; branch position; node age; rooting percentage; days to root; root mass or length; transplant survival; morphology after establishment.

Record rooting percentage, time to visible root or establishment, losses, abnormal growth, environmental conditions, treatment differences, and follow-up observations that would confirm or revise the interpretation.

misconceptions: Taking a new cutting resets all biological history.
Revegetated material is automatically rejuvenated and superior.
evidenceLimits: Cannabis-specific evidence on formal rejuvenation and phase change is limited. Do not claim a universal maximum mother age or clone generation without controlled data.

knowledgeCheck: For "Juvenility, Maturity, and Cutting Competence", explain the mechanism behind this objective: Explain how ontogenetic age, tissue position, donor condition, and genotype affect a cutting’s competence to form roots. Which observation or measurement would best test whether that mechanism is operating in the real crop?

A learner claims, "Calendar age alone predicts rooting." Use the lesson's science and evidence limits to explain why that claim is unreliable, then name one observation or measurement that could separate the competing explanations.

Applied case — Standardize donor age class, branch position, node number, harvest interval, and mother-management history during trials. Rotate or rehabilitate mothers only after comparing propagation and crop performance. Build a verification plan using the lesson's record set (Controlled record set: Mother age and propagation generation; vegetative or reproductive history; branch position; node age; rooting percentage; days to root; root mass or length; transplant survival; morphology after establishment.). What would you compare before and after the action, and what result would make you revise the original interpretation?
